text: Rarely has corporate behavior been subject to such intense scrutiny as it is today, with consumers, regulators, and employees alike demanding greater transparency from the companies they support. Nevertheless, ethical conduct is often easier to promise in a code of conduct than to practice under financial pressure. Consider a firm that, in order to cut corners on safety, quietly turns a blind eye to compliance failures; should an accident occur, the organization may find itself liable for damages far exceeding whatever it saved. Nor is exploitative behavior confined to factory floors: overworked employees, denied any semblance of work-life balance, frequently report exhaustion, while nepotism and unresolved conflicts of interest continue to undermine trust in promotion decisions. A whistleblower who dares to speak up about such practices, meanwhile, risks retaliation, however illegal such treatment may technically be. Genuine corporate social responsibility, then, requires more than incentivizing good behavior with an annual sustainability report; it demands accountability even when downsizing or layoffs make short-term profit tempting. Companies that merely appear ethical, without changing underlying practices, are increasingly being exposed by an informed and skeptical public unwilling to accept appearances alone.
